text:
Spinach.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn / Winter

Spinach can give quick leafy crops through much of the year, but needs rich soil and steady moisture to avoid bolting. True spinach has summer and winter forms. New Zealand spinach is a separate, frost-tender summer substitute for hot weather; perpetual spinach (spinach beet) is a leaf beet. Match type to season and pick tender leaves regularly.

Quick facts
Sow

True spinach mid-Mar–May for summer leaves, Aug–Sep for winter.

Harvest

May – Mar

Germination

12–20 days

Sowing depth

1 in.

Row spacing

True spinach: 8 in.

Yield (10 ft row)

5-10 lb

Plant spacing

True spinach: thin to 3 in., then harvest alternates to leave about 6 in. Baby leaves need little thinning.

Ready in

From sowing: baby leaves ~4 weeks; mature leaves ~8; longer in cold weather

New Zealand spinach

Sow after frost, usually late May.

Recommended varieties
SUMMER
Medania

Familiar true spinach with generous green leaves for salads or cooking.

SUMMER
Matador

Slow-bolting, deep-green, succulent leaves. Sow small batches for a steady supply.

SUMMER
Monterey F1

Quick hybrid with dark leaves and downy-mildew resistance. Suits warm-season outdoor and protected winter crops.

WINTER
Giant Winter

Hardy, large-leaved spinach for cooler seasons, complementing spring/early-summer crops.

Key risks
Bolting

Heat, long days and dry soil can trigger flowering.

Mould or downy mildew

Yellow upper-leaf patches with grey-purple mould below can indicate downy mildew.

New Zealand spinach frost

New Zealand spinach is frost-tender.

Manganese deficiency

Yellowing between veins can have several causes.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
84
SALADS & LEAVES

Keep true spinach cool and moist.

Rich soil and timely thinning help plants keep producing tender leaves.

Match the crop to the season.

Winter spinach and frost-tender New Zealand spinach need different treatment.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil improved with compost. Aim for pH 6–6.5; test before liming and avoid over-liming.
Summer true spinach likes part shade; winter crops need sun. New Zealand spinach likes warmth; protect from frost.
Sowing & planting
Sow true spinach
Thin young plants
True spinach 

Choose a variety suited to the season. Sow short drills 1 in. deep in succession. Use ridges on wet ground for the winter crop.

New Zealand spinach 

This spreading crop needs more room. Soak seeds for 24 hours, sow three per spot and keep the strongest. Allow 2 ft between plants and 3–4 ft between rows.

Looking after the crop
Thin true spinach promptly. Weed, mulch and water in dry spells, especially in summer.
Use hardy winter varieties; protect with cloches in cold areas and ventilate in mild weather. Pick lightly in slow winter growth. Replace bolted true spinach with a suitable new sowing.
Keep the strongest New Zealand seedling at each station and harvest regularly once warm-weather growth is established.
Harvesting & storage
Pick young outer leaves lightly from several plants, leaving growing centres intact for regrowth. Never strip one bare; take winter leaves sparingly.
Cut young shoots from New Zealand spinach little and often. True spinach cooks down considerably, so allow enough plants for useful pickings.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	Plants run to seed in heat or dry soil.	Keep soil moist; sow small replacement rows in suitable cool conditions.
Mould or downy mildew	Yellow patches above; grey mould below.	Remove affected leaves; clear badly diseased crops and rotate.
New Zealand spinach frost	Frost damages or kills this tender substitute.	Sow or plant New Zealand spinach after frost danger has passed.
Manganese deficiency	Leaves yellow in over-limed, high-pH soil.	Check the cause and pH; avoid further unnecessary lime.
Leaf spot	Pale-centred spots with dark or purple rims.	Remove diseased leaves and debris; rotate and avoid crowding.
Spinach blight	Young leaves yellow, pucker and become narrow.	Remove infected plants; clear weed hosts and monitor aphids.
Final tips

Use tender thinnings in the kitchen instead of letting seedlings crowd one another.

Have a replacement short row ready when heat or flowering ends a true-spinach crop.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
